analysis.one_liner: Bans charging unconscionably high prices for emergency supplies sold to responders during federally declared disasters.
analysis.headline: The anti-price-gouging bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared emergency or disaster, this bill would have made it illegal to charge responders — state agencies, hospitals, and nonprofits buying supplies for the emergency — more than 10% above the average pre-emergency price, unless the increase reflected actual costs. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the ban in court. The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, hospitals, and nonprofits responding to disasters and public health emergencies would buy masks, ventilators, generators, and other emergency goods at normal prices instead of inflated ones, stretching limited emergency budgets further. Taxpayers ultimately benefit too, since public money funds much of that purchasing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Emergency responders and the communities they serve

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful to charge more than 10% above the pre-emergency average price (unless the increase reflects actual costs) for emergency supplies sold to responders during a federally declared emergency.
It gives the FTC and state attorneys general power to sue for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution, giving states a federal backstop against gouging.

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of emergency supplies — retailers, wholesalers, and distributors — who could no longer raise prices sharply above pre-emergency levels during federally declared emergencies.

drawbacks.text: The bright-line rule (any price over 10% above the pre-emergency average, unless justified by costs) could penalize sellers whose costs genuinely rose in an emergency, and could discourage suppliers from shipping goods into affected areas if they fear enforcement.
The bill covers only purchases by responders (government agencies, hospitals, and nonprofits), so price gouging sold directly to individual consumers would not be covered by this Act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — responders buying masks, ventilators, generators, and other supplies at normal prices during emergencies — is real but limited to federally declared emergencies and to goods bought by responders rather than consumers directly. The main drawback is the enforcement burden on sellers and possible reduced supply in affected areas if sellers hold back goods rather than risk penalties under a bright-line 10% rule. On balance it is a narrow, well-targeted consumer protection, but it never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection subcommittee on February 2-3, 2021, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jackie Speier introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, with five original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where it stayed.
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of emergency supplies are better off, since they face no federal limit on emergency-period price increases beyond the state laws that already existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Emergency-supply sellers; no federal price limits

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six cosponsors.

for.name: 7 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never advanced far enough for a party-split vote to occur; committee inaction rather than any recorded vote ended it.

industries.industry: Retailers, distributors, and suppliers of emergency goods (medical supplies, generators, protective equipment)
industries.note: During federally declared emergencies they could no longer raise prices more than 10% above the prior 30-day average on goods sold to responders without documenting real cost increases. Emergency-period windfall pricing would become legally risky.
